strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem with a sensible modular approach: detect problematic seam regions, refine their alignment, and reconnect the local seams. This could improve existing pipelines without retraining or redesigning their alignment methods.

Tables 1–2 demonstrate consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods, five initial alignment methods, and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, baseline SSIM on SEAGULL improves from 0.638 to 0.697, supporting the module’s usefulness across different configurations.

Figures 1, 5, and 7 provide qualitative evidence of repaired structural discontinuities. Flow attenuation and constrained local seam merging address a meaningful difficulty in reinserting corrected patches.

The pipeline figures and pseudocode make the approach understandable. The manuscript attributes its principal methods and existing datasets, provides a code link, and includes parameter ablations and a useful failure analysis.
weaknesses: The main evidence measures agreement between image patches along the seam, which does not adequately assess the quality of the complete mosaic after warping. Table 3 exposes this limitation: removing the sigmoid improves most reported metrics despite introducing acknowledged boundary artifacts. An independent assessment of perceptual quality, structural distortion, or patch-boundary continuity is needed to establish that the numerical improvements translate reliably into better mosaics.

The contribution beyond existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. LPAM combines established SSIM, Otsu thresholding, SIFT flow, and graph-cut components, but the distinction from SEAGULL [22] and dense-matching-based seam estimation [35] needs stronger analysis and comparisons. Figure 7 supplies only one scene for the end-to-end comparison with Parallax and SEAGULL; Table 2 evaluates UDIS++ only as an initial aligner. The experiments therefore establish an effective add-on more clearly than a substantially new stitching paradigm.

The seam acceptance rule in Section 3.2 has a concrete failure case: max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts any uniformly high-error seam. It cannot distinguish uniformly good alignment from uniformly poor alignment, and the paper provides no absolute-error safeguard or evaluation of this detector. Together with the patch-support failure in Figure 6, this limits the claim that seam quality is dissociated from initial alignment accuracy.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Section 4.4 reports LPAM time separately from host seam-cutting time; its roughly 6–10 seconds of additional computation is comparable to or greater than several host methods’ costs. For example, the SEAGULL baseline takes 4.11 seconds and LPAM adds 7.34 seconds. Total pipeline timings and scaling with resolution and corrected area would better substantiate the description of the module as lightweight.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the supplied manuscript despite the code link. SIFT-flow settings, correction-patch padding and overlap handling, input resizing, and the custom dataset’s collection and selection protocol are insufficiently specified. Several additional comparisons and computational breakdowns are deferred to supplementary material that is absent from the supplied PDF.
